explanation:
## The program

```cpp
void swapInts(int& a, int& b)
{
    int temp{ a };
    a = b;
    b = temp;
}
```

## A reference is another name, not a copy

```
void f(int  n)      n is a new variable, initialised from the argument
void f(int& n)      n is the argument, under a second name
```

Everything else follows from that one sentence. Assigning to `n`
in the second case assigns to the caller’s variable, because they
are the same object. There is no pointer to dereference and no
syntax at the call site — `f(x)` either way.

C++ before references had only the pointer version:

```cpp
void swapInts(int* a, int* b)
{
    int t{ *a };
    *a = *b;
    *b = t;
}

swapInts(&x, &y);      // the & at the call site says "may be changed"
```

which is noisier and has one advantage: the caller can see it. With
references the call looks like any other, which is why a reference
parameter that is not `const` is worth a second look when you read
a declaration.

## Why the temporary is needed

```cpp
a = b;      // a is now 8; the old 3 is gone
b = a;      // b is now 8 as well
```

The first assignment destroys the value the second one needed. A
swap of two variables always needs somewhere to put one of them —
either a third variable, or one of the arithmetic tricks
(`a += b; b = a - b; a -= b;`) which are shorter, slower, harder to
read, and overflow. Use the temporary.

## There is already one

`std::swap(a, b)` from `<utility>` does this for any type, and is
what you should call in real code. Writing it once by hand is the
point here, because it is the shortest possible program that shows
what a reference parameter is for.

## What this does not check

Calling it with the same variable twice — `swapInts(x, x)`. Both
references then name one object, the three assignments still work
out correctly, and the value is unchanged. Not every function with
two reference parameters survives that, and a function that cannot
is said not to be *self-assignment safe*.
